body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Risk-based versus fixed six-month dental recall in adults: a multicentre randomised trial","authors":"Oyelaran-MacLeod S, Brandt-Ishikawa P, Nystrom-Achebe K","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Dental Practice Research","doi":"10.5555/jdpr.2020.0233","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 2,380 adults attending 51 general dental practices to recall intervals set by an individual risk assessment or to fixed six-month recall, and followed them for four years. Caries increment did not differ between groups (mean difference 0.1 decayed, missing or filled surfaces). In the risk-based group, 41 percent of adults were assigned intervals of 12 months or longer. Gum health and patient satisfaction were similar. Practices found the risk assessment took about two minutes per patient once staff were trained."},{"title":"How dentists set recall intervals: a cross-sectional analysis of 12,000 patient records","authors":"Kowalski-Adebayo J, Hartley-Nguyen L","year":2017,"venue":"Community Dental Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined the most recent examination records of 12,000 adults in 30 general dental practices. In all, 81 percent of adults had a six-month recall interval regardless of their recorded risk category, and the risk field was completed in 64 percent of records. Adults recorded as low risk were as likely to receive six-month recall as those recorded as high risk. Practices paid per course of treatment set shorter intervals than salaried services. The analysis could not tell whether dentists assessed risk without recording it."},{"title":"Completeness of caries risk assessment in dental records: an audit across 40 practices","authors":"Mbatha-Lindgren C, Fitzroy-Okafor D","year":2022,"venue":"Dental Records and Governance","doi":"10.5555/drg.2022.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We audited 4,000 adult dental records from 40 practices for the presence and currency of a caries risk assessment. The risk field was blank in 29 percent of records. Among patients with two assessments, the second was copied forward unchanged in 47 percent, even when new fillings had been placed between visits. Practices using structured templates had fewer blank fields. The audit did not examine whether recall intervals followed the recorded risk. Blank fields were more common in the records of patients who attended irregularly."},{"title":"Recall intervals between routine dental examinations: national clinical guideline","authors":"National Dental Guidance Committee","year":2015,"venue":"National Clinical Guideline Series","doi":"10.5555/ncgs.2015.0019","providerType":"guideline","abstract":"The committee recommends that the interval between routine dental examinations is set for each patient between 3 and 24 months for adults, based on an assessment of disease risk at each examination, and that the interval is reviewed at every visit. The evidence for particular intervals was judged to be of low certainty, and the recommendation rests largely on expert consensus. The committee asked for research on how intervals are set in practice and on the views of patients. It also advises that patients are told the reason for the interval chosen."},{"title":"Patients' views on longer dental recall intervals: an interview study","authors":"Rossi-Achterberg N, Oduya-Winter H","year":2019,"venue":"Oral Health Perspectives","doi":"10.5555/ohp.2019.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We interviewed 28 adults who had been offered a recall interval longer than six months. Most accepted the longer interval once the reason was explained, but several worried that problems would be missed or that they would lose their place at the practice. Participants who paid for treatment welcomed fewer visits, while those exempt from charges valued regular contact. Few participants knew that a risk assessment had been done. Some said they would prefer to agree the interval together with the dentist."},{"title":"Deprivation and recall intervals in general dental practice: an analysis of routine records","authors":"Tanaka-Whitlock E, Mensah-Carlsson R","year":2024,"venue":"Community Dental Practice","doi":"10.5555/cdp.2024.0102","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed routine records of 38,500 adults in 22 practices by area deprivation. Adults in the most deprived quintile were more likely to have no recall interval recorded (19 percent against 7 percent in the least deprived quintile). Where an interval was recorded, adults in the most deprived quintile were slightly more often given six months. Missed appointments were more common in deprived areas and often led to the interval being left blank. The analysis had no clinical measure of risk."},{"title":"Caries increment by recall interval in low-risk adults: a practice-based cohort","authors":"Leclerc-Bamidele A, Sorensen-Pike J","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Dental Practice Research","doi":"10.5555/jdpr.2021.0310","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 1,640 adults assessed as low risk for three years in 18 practices that had adopted risk-based recall. Adults recalled at 12 to 24 months had a similar caries increment to those recalled at six months (0.4 against 0.3 surfaces over three years). Adults who missed two consecutive recalls had the largest increment. Follow-up data were incomplete for 23 percent of adults who changed practice. The authors conclude that longer intervals appear safe for low-risk adults who keep attending, and that missed recalls matter more than the interval itself."},{"title":"Recall interval setting under activity-based dental contracts: a commissioning briefing","authors":"Regional Dental Commissioning Unit","year":null,"venue":"Commissioning briefing series","providerType":"report","abstract":"This briefing describes how activity-based dental contracts can discourage longer recall intervals, because each examination counts towards contracted activity. It summarises local audits suggesting that most adults are recalled at six months and proposes that commissioners measure the distribution of recall intervals by recorded risk before changing contracts. The briefing gives no publication date and its local audits are not referenced in detail. It suggests that practices serving deprived areas face the greatest tension between access targets and longer intervals."}]}
